title: Champollion reads the hieroglyphs — Lettre à M. Dacier, 1822
sources: Wikipedia: Lettre à M. Dacier — 14 September 1822 breakthrough while visiting his brother; 'Je tiens l'affaire!' ('I've got it!') then fainted; 27 September 1822 presented to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres

Wikipedia: Jean-François Champollion — fluent in Coptic, which he rightly believed was the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language; many thought hieroglyphs were esoteric symbols that could not be deciphered; Thomas Young (London) read only some signs; breakthrough 14 September 1822 comparing texts from Abu Simbel; ran down the street to find his brother, yelled 'I've got it!' and collapsed; read the letter before the assembled Académie with Young present; congratulated by the audience including Young; relationship quickly deteriorated as Young felt denied credit

Wikipedia: Rosetta Stone — decree of 196 BC in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; found in July 1799 by French soldiers during Napoleon's invasion of Egypt; script not understood since shortly before the fall of the Roman Empire, last known hieroglyphic inscription AD 394

post.facebook:
On this day in 1822, a young Frenchman announced he could read a script that had been lost for fourteen centuries.

Napoleon's soldiers had found the key in Egypt in 1799: the Rosetta Stone, one decree carved in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. Yet many scholars believed hieroglyphs were mystic symbols that could never be read. In London, Thomas Young had worked out only a few signs.

Jean-François Champollion had an edge: he spoke Coptic, the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language. On 14 September 1822 it clicked. He ran down the street to find his brother, shouted “I've got it!” — and collapsed.

Thirteen days later he read his Letter to M. Dacier before the Académie in Paris. In the audience sat his rival, Thomas Young, who congratulated him. Soon, the two were quarrelling over who deserved the credit.
